blocks.x: Regular Business
24-000632 — Site Plan Approval Extension — 4 & 7 Kidder Lane, Quaker Lane Associates
Discussion Summary

Craig Burtis (Acorn Engineering) requested a one-year extension of the April 2025 site plan approval (amended September 2025). A site plan is the detailed plan for a building project, which the Planning Board reviews. The project is a 110-unit mixed-use redevelopment at the end of Kidder Lane. It also includes a westerly extension of the River Walk Trail.
Construction is now set to begin this fall. It follows a phased schedule coordinated with the adjacent Saccarappa Park project.

Phase 1 covers demolition, utility installation, the main storm drain runs, and replacement of a 48-inch stormwater pipe under Dana Street. That pipe is now specified in high-density polyethylene plastic rather than concrete (lighter, easier to handle, comparable lifespan, lower cost).

Erosion control along the Presumpscot River goes in this fall and is re-inspected before Phase 2 begins, likely in spring 2027. That phase tackles the stormwater tree filters, rain garden, and remaining site work.

City Planner Rebecca Spitella explained that the phased approach lets the applicant post a smaller performance guarantee for the fall utility/demolition work alone. (A performance guarantee is a financial guarantee that the work will be finished.) The full project guarantee is required once Phase 2 begins. No substantive changes were made to the underlying conditions of approval, other than triggers tied to each phase.
Vice Chair Turcotte confirmed that this is the applicant's first extension request and voiced no objection given the project's size.
Nancy Litrocapes was previously recused from this project. (To recuse is to step out of a vote because of a conflict of interest.) She asked whether she needed to recuse again for an extension vote.
Staff advised that she could vote if she felt she could remain impartial to the extension itself. She confirmed support. No public comment.
Key Decisions
Approved unanimously by roll call; all nine present, including both alternates, voted in favor. Moved by John Turcotte, seconded by Kevin Price.
Action Items
None.
New Business
26-000527 — Site Plan, Final Vote — 3 Saunders Way, Bill Dodge Kia
Discussion Summary

Dustin Roma (DM Roma Consulting Engineers) returned with the final site plan for the Bill Dodge Kia renovation, first workshopped July 7. It includes a 2,160-sq-ft service-area addition and a 3,850-sq-ft showroom addition. It also includes updated Kia branding and signage, including a new pylon sign sized to code through Code Enforcement.

Other parts are new electric vehicle charging stations and landscaping improvements at the corner nearest the adjacent Infinity dealership. The landscaping adds new trees, shrubs, and perennials replacing a plain grass-and-evergreen strip, to match the Infinity building's more developed landscaping.
One existing light pole is removed for the expansion. A second, inside a retained landscaped island, stays. There are no changes to overall site circulation.
Staff had no additions. Chair McWilliams asked whether the building signage would be illuminated. Roma confirmed internal illumination, useful given early winter darkness.
The Chair called the renovation a nice addition to the corridor. No public comment.
Key Decisions
Approved unanimously by roll call; all nine present, including both alternates, voted yes. Moved by Kevin Price, seconded by Karen Axelson.
Action Items
None.
26-000275 — Site Plan, Subdivision, Conditional Use — Marco Commons, 547 Saco St.
Discussion Summary
Dustin Roma presented the first phase of “Marco Commons.” It subdivides the remaining land at 547 Saco St. into three new lots.

An existing farmhouse lot was already separated off. The developer donated it to Calvary Church, which uses it as a residential facility for a faith-based recovery program. Staff said it does not meet the definition of a treatment facility that would require approvals.
Lot 1 is a tight envelope reserved for a possible future single-family home around an existing barn.
Lot 2 is sized for a future duplex.
Lot 3 is the subject of tonight's site plan. It has two 12-unit multifamily buildings, moved as far as possible from the southern property line to preserve more of the existing tree buffer.
All three lots share one private driveway off Saco Street.

An informational master plan shown for context (not for approval) depicts an eventual full build-out of seven 12-unit buildings, 84 total units. The build-out would go at roughly two buildings per year.

This phase builds sidewalk along the property's frontage (the length of the lot along the street), a crosswalk with a rapid-flashing beacon, and curbing. The curbing runs along the full roughly 1,300-foot Saco Street sidewalk gap, ahead of a paving moratorium. The city agreed to negotiate the private easements (rights to use part of someone else's land) that the full sidewalk needs. The developer builds the rest of the sidewalk in its next phase.

The Recreation and Conservation Commission accepted this sidewalk work plus an internal trail loop as satisfying the open-space requirement. Staff recommended against a public trail connection through the private development. They cited recurring conflict elsewhere in the city when that has been tried.
Key Decisions

Approved unanimously by roll call (subdivision and Lot 3 site plan for two 12-unit buildings); all nine present, including both alternates, voted yes. Moved by Vice Chair John Turcotte, seconded by Robin Tannenbaum. The board separately voted unanimously, by the same nine, to move into workshop session for the remaining agenda items, moved by Nancy Litrocapes, seconded by Kevin Price.
Action Items
None.
Point / Counterpoint
“… although we've heard 184 planned units out back. I'm sure everybody can do the math and figure out they're gonna be equal or more than those numbers of vehicles entering and leaving Saco Street.”
“Is that it's not 184, it's 84. There's seven, seven twelve-unit buildings. The full build out, the full master plan [is] 84.”
blocks.cite: Rebecca Spitella, City Planner (correcting the record)

blocks.x: “Respectfully, saying that a one-bedroom apartment is going to be cheaper than a two-bedroom apartment is not affordable housing ... I expect that these one bedrooms will be at least $2,000 a month for rent, and that's simply not affordable.”
“If you rotated building A 180 degrees [to put] the shed in the back, and building B rotated at ninety degrees clockwise ... it would look like two different buildings, but it's the same building.”
blocks.cite: Jason Frazier, Board Member (on the mechanical sheds facing the lot)

26-000635 — Site Plan — 100 Larrabee Road, 100 Larrabee LLC
Discussion Summary

Henry Hess (Sebago Technics) presented a 33–34-space parking expansion at the Larrabee Complex (currently 333 spaces). It is driven by new tenant leases and recent evening programming that has created congestion. Most new spaces go in along the western Terminal Street side via a shifted driveway entrance.

A new one-way directional pattern near the rear drop-off area is intended to reduce crisscrossing traffic at peak times. Several board members tied that peak-time traffic to a tenant dance studio's evening classes.
The roughly 6,000-sq-ft paving expansion requires two new stormwater detention basins. It removes four or five existing trees, to be replaced as the formal site plan develops.

The expansion drops the site's landscaped-area percentage from an already-nonconforming 14% to 12%. (Nonconforming means allowed to stay although it no longer meets current zoning.) The Gateway Commercial District's standard is 25%.
Staff explained that the district allows this if the board finds no reasonable alternative. That triggers a fee-in-lieu payment, a fee paid instead of meeting the requirement.

The fee uses the same formula as the open-space fee-in-lieu. It goes to Main Street corridor safety/beautification improvements. It is preliminarily estimated at about $13,071, pending a finalized number.

There is an unresolved Fire Department objection. The staff memo flagged that the Fire Department does not support several proposed spaces in front of a building entrance, on life-safety grounds. Staff confirmed the board generally follows Fire Department guidance. The applicant acknowledged that the concern will be addressed before a formal site plan.

Member Jason Frazier suggested swapping underused Larrabee Road frontage parking for landscaping, shifting that capacity to the rear. Chair McWilliams proposed that fee-in-lieu funds from projects like this be earmarked for a dedicated tree/landscaping fund rather than a general appearance fund. No public comment.
Key Decisions
No vote — workshop item.
Action Items
None.
Point / Counterpoint

“As someone who's cut it a little close on dropping off a daughter at a dance here ... you have people leaving and coming at the same time. Circulation is a challenge ... it's been more than once of like, nope, you can't run in, stop, car.”
blocks.cite: Member Kevin Price (on dance-studio pickup/dropoff congestion)

blocks.x: 26-000630 — Site Plan, Subdivision — 267 Conant Street, MGM Builders
Discussion Summary

Dustin Roma reintroduced a property last brought before the board roughly five to six years ago. It was then an all-commercial development that stalled before final approval due to a paving moratorium conflict.

The revived concept proposes three multifamily buildings totaling 36 units. It also proposes a 4,000-sq-ft pad site reserved for a future commercial building (no tenant yet identified) along Conant Street.
The design has a “main street”-style storefront appearance. It has ample landscaped setback (the required distance between buildings and the property line). Parking is kept behind all structures.

Staff noted that the property had been thought to be split-zoned. It was fully reclassified into the City Center district in an earlier board-initiated rezoning cleanup. That gives the applicant more room to move buildings than the original stalled plan assumed.
The project extends the Conant Street sidewalk east to connect with an adjacent condo development's own recent extension.

Several board members raised concerns about the heavy, undifferentiated parking area and the lack of visual relationship between the two residential buildings. They encouraged the applicant to continue refining the layout before returning with a full application. No public comment.
Key Decisions
No vote — workshop item.
Action Items
None.
Point / Counterpoint

“It's a tough one ... to lay out. But I find ... you talked about that heavy parking area ... it's very not residential ... I just wonder if there's more work that can be done to separate the residential component from the commercial component ... to make it feel residential.”
“As long as ... you make an effort at that look and there will be some landscape between ... I think that's gonna be a good look from Conant Street.”
26-000636 — Subdivision — 108 Longfellow Street, Longfellow 108 LLC
Discussion Summary

Dustin Roma presented a straightforward three-lot subdivision of a 1.7-acre parcel, with no physical development proposed at this stage. The existing three-unit multifamily building's driveway easement would be conveyed in fee (transferred as full ownership) to the eventual owner of the adjacent lot. That lot is currently undeveloped, has zoning capacity for roughly nine units under current rules, and has an undetermined use. This lets that owner improve shared access on its own land.

The lot nearest the steep slope above an abutting (neighboring) property was deliberately drawn with a small building envelope sized only for a single-family home. Any development beyond that would require a separate surface drainage plan review. So would development of three or more units on the other lot. Anything of three-plus units would also need a return trip to this board.
The applicant hoped to return with a full application in September.

Abutters Larry Mac and Marshall Mac (Mac Brothers, whose family property includes a 90-unit elderly-housing project and a historic building nearby) raised drainage concerns. They rooted them in the site's history (the back road follows a former canal) and a high water table. They asked that any future development account for added runoff onto their property.

Staff confirmed that any future lot development must go through surface drainage plan review. Staff also confirmed that the small lot meets minimum zoning dimension standards. Chair McWilliams separately flagged a resident's written concern about invasive Japanese knotweed on the site, for attention whenever future development occurs.
Key Decisions
No vote — workshop item.
Action Items
None.
Point / Counterpoint

“We have a 90-unit [elderly] housing project ... and uh that our back road there was actually the canal ... it's a high water table, the whole area down below ... as far as Area three, I don't have a problem with that ... but area one especially is a problem for us. So that needs to be addressed.”
blocks.cite: Marshall Mac, abutting property owner (Mac Brothers)
